maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. 300, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words on the bill I think I should first commend the minister for introducing it. Each of the amendments in the bill is a definite step forward, either for the protection of the travelling public who use our deep-sea and coastal steamers, or for the improvement of working conditions of the men who serve on those ships.
Some regret may be expressed that all the amendments which might be considered desirable at this time have not been proposed, but certainly a good forward step has been taken.
The minister in his speech used what to me was a startling phrase when he said that seamen had always been favourites of the law. I think that most of us who recall stories of the sea which we read as boys, or who have had some knowledge of the conditions under which

our merchant marine seamen work, will be inclined to think that, far from being the favourites of the law, seamen have been favourites for the attention of the law, and that the law which protected the ordinary civilian worker did not afford the same protection for seamen at sea.
The reason for this is a simple one. The master of a ship at sea can scarcely be compared to the manager of an industrial plant ashore, because the manager of a plant ashore has both the police force and the ordinary courts of the country to enforce infractions of the civil or criminal code, whereas the master of a ship at sea has no such help. Moreover, he has the direct responsibility for the lives of all those under him. And so great power was given him. But often with that power there was great abuse, and unfortunately the seamen did not enjoy the protection of the law courts of the country which other groups have had.
Since there are few maritime members, not much attention is paid to seamen's problems. Certainly no one in this house has talked a quarter as much about the seamen of Canada as prairie members have talked about coarse grains. What advantage the seaman has obtained in recent years has been won by himself through seamen's unions in Great Britain, the United States and this country. Whatever improvements have been made, the seamen themselves were the ones to force the issue. They are a difficult group to organize, because of the shifting nature of their employment, and they have been many times at the mercy of the shipowners. The result of course has been to render seafaring not very attractive to the average young Canadian. Too many of our ships are manned by men who did not begin to follow the sea as a career but rather drifted into the occupation, which is not healthy for any form of employment. The efforts of the unions, however, have lifted the lot of the average seafarer and also made the vocation a more attractive one so far as the average Canadian is concerned.
It will be some time, however, before wages and working conditions of the average Canadian seaman will equal those of the Canadian industrial worker, and this for a simple reason. Our seamen come into immediate competition with those of every other nation. It is all very well in Canada, within our single economic union, to lift the working conditions and pay of competing industrial workers, but when Canadian seamen manning Canadian ships have to compete with the ships and seamen of other countries, a very different situation arises.

Canada Shipping Act
Senator Paterson put on the record of the upper house the wages paid today to ablebodied deep-sea seamen of various nations.
I should like to run over it. The able-bodied seaman in the United States receives $192 per month plus board. Canada is the next highest, paying $170. Look at the other countries with whom we have to compete: Norway, $101, the United Kingdom $96, Sweden $86, Denmark $85, the Netherlands $74, France $79, Yugoslavia $84. Shipowners therefore - have a difficult problem in trying to keep Canadian ships in competition against the low wages paid by their competitors.
One of the recent grievances of Canadian seamen has been the fact that though while at sea they accepted ship's discipline, they felt that they should not be under ship's discipline when at home in Canadian ports. The Canada Shipping Act provided that if they left the ship in a Canadian port without being paid off they were deserters and liable to imprisonment, a condition which does not affect the ordinary worker who decides that he does not want to work any longer for a certain plant and leaves it. I am pleased to see an amendment designed to change this condition, so that once the ship has got into a Canadian port and has been properly secured, the Canadian seaman will have the same right to leave his employment as the Canadian industrial worker. There is also provision for proper qualification and certification of Canadian seamen, and this is a positive forward step.
I mentioned earlier that too often the seafarer has drifted into his occupation. Any steps taken to recognize his occupation and to lift its standards will make it a more attractive one, and the provision for a permanent register of certification of able-bodied seamen will be welcome.
I think that this measure might have contained a provision for the training of apprentice seamen such as the Scandinavian countries and Great Britain have provided in the past. The best way to attract young men to the merchant marine as a career is to provide them with merchant marine training on floating training schools such as the Scandinavian countries and the United Kingdom provide for their young men.
The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) said that the provision of a continuous discharge book for seamen was the one bad spot in the bill-an amendment, incidentally, introduced by the senate; but I do not agree with this view. I would regard this as one of the good things in the bill, in that a-continuous discharge book is a valuable record for the good seaman. At present with individual voyage discharge slips if he has 5849-256J
a bad record on discharge he can destroy that slip, which he cannot do with a continuous discharge book on which the entry of his character and qualifications is made by the master. At the end of each voyage, if his record is good, it will do two things. First of all it is the record of a good seaman which he can use to advantage in seeking future employment either afloat or ashore, and secondly, it is an added protection to the public, because, the good seaman being more likely to get employment, it means that ships are better manned. I would heartily support the new change providing for a continuous discharge book, and I hope too that in the discharge book the method the British use for recording qualifications will not be followed. In the British marine a seaman can only be assessed as "very good" by the master, or the master can decline to report on him. There is too great a gap between a good seaman, an average seaman and an inferior seaman. I think the rating which the Royal Navy uses and which goes from exceptional to superior, satisfactory, fair, or unsatisfactory, would be a better range and would be a better assessment for the seaman and for the shipping master hiring seamen.
There is one other feature about such a classification. It is a real assistance to discipline. Today some seamen do not care how they are discharged, whether their discharge slip is bad or good, for they can destroy it if it is bad. But with a continuous discharge book many a seaman for fear of a bad discharge will conduct himself better and be of more help on the ship than he would if he knew that, at the end of the voyage, he could tear up his discharge if it is unsatisfactory.
The provision for the right of the dependents of a seaman to launch an action in case of a fatal accident is another step in bringing the seaman as a worker more in line with industrial workers in Canada. The dependents of the industrial worker for some years have had the right to sue the employer in the case of an accident which resulted in the death of the breadwinner. The provision to extend that right now to the dependents of the seamen is another forward step.
The schedules at the end of the bill are also improvements. There is provision for medical examination of the men on the ship before they start on a voyage. That is certainly an excellent practice to follow in any industry where the men are at such close quarters for long periods of time. The provision for examination of the food and the certification of the cooks is another excellent one. I know that at home in
Canada Shipping Act

British Columbia, in our mines and logging camps, the morale of the camp pretty well depends on the ability of the cook. That condition is, I imagine, even more marked at sea. The proper qualification of cooks, certification before they embark on voyages, and the examination of food, will do much to improve the working conditions of the men who are afloat.
Having said some agreeable things about what the bill contains, perhaps I should express regret that there are certain provisions it does not contain.
The people of British Columbia and the daily press have been most anxious to obtain better protection in the way of radiotelegraph for our coastal steamers. We have had two or three wrecks with fatalities in recent years, partly attributable to lack of rescue equipment and lack of proper radio services to attract rescue equipment. There are two things about British Columbia, of which perhaps eastern members are not aware, although we British Columbians try to keep others well posted on the virtues and qualities of our province. One thing is the large volume of coastal passenger traffic we have on our coast. The reasons are fairly obvious. We have no north Or south road along the British Columbia coast; the most northerly road ends thirteen miles north of the city of Vancouver. Many people in the city of Vancouver have never been on a train, but have nevertheless travelled up to Alaska and down to California by boat.
The second thing is the fact that we have many islands-one very large one. It is not perhaps as famous as the island in the maritimes, but it is bigger in point of size, population and wealth. Vancouver island has a population of 200,000. Access back and forth between the mainland and these islands is naturally by boat. We have in addition a great volume of traffic, particularly in the summer, up and down the mainland coast. Most of the people on the lower mainland have summer homes or spend summer holidays in little resorts on the lower hundred miles of coast. One of the heaviest movements of people up and down the coast occurs in the summer months, the little coastal boats often carrying 1,500 and 2,000 people. Then there is the United States deep-sea traffic plying between United States cities and Alaska, in which use is made of our waters. For these reasons we have a much heavier coastal passenger traffic, I think, than any other part of Canada.
The second point I raise is the nature of our coast. Of course at times we are prone to use ecstatic terms about our mountains, inlets

and islands, our blue seas, and so on. But these things have another side. The coast of British Columbia is heavily indented by long fiords-there are thousands of little islands, reefs and shoals, strong tides and winds-and is an extremely dangerous coast to navigate. The very low record of wrecks we have had in the past has been attributable mainly to the great skill of our navigators. They get little help from lights or signals, and some navigators call it the black coast. If you come up north by water from Seattle in the state of Washington to the United States border, there is never a time that you cannot see a light behind and a light ahead. Once you come to the British Columbia coast, navigation lights are few and far between. It is the rare stretch where you can sight one light. Having left one light behind, you maintain a reckoned course as best you can, allowing for wind and tide, until you open up the next light. The disastrous accident we had last fall with the loss of the Gulf Stream was the result of failure to open a hidden light. Passing on to the north, once you get past the Alaska border, again the seaway is almost as bright as the main street in a city. These conditions-the blackness of our coast, the narrow inlets and many islands, our long fiords, our heavy rain in winter, and even worse, our fogs, all combine to make coastal traffic on the British Columbia coast a matter of proceeding through perilous waters. That is why we feel that the coastal traffic should be protected in every possible way, especially by sufficient wireless apparatus and operators to enable a call for assistance to go out in case a boat strikes a reef, a rock or another boat, and a disaster occurs.
It was the intention that the Canada Shipping Act should provide such protection, because there is a provision, which is in the original bill although it is not included in the amending bill, to the effect that any ship carrying fifty or more passengers more than 200 miles from place to place, must carry a radiotelegraph operator. If the ship carries 250 or more passengers, it can go only ninety miles without a telegraph operator, and a ship carrying more than 500 passengers can go only twenty miles without a telegraph operator. I presume that clause was framed with good intentions, but the steamship companies get around it in an easy way. The framers of the act, when they used the phrase "from place to place", were probably thinking in terms of proper harbours to which a ship could return when in distress, and from which aid could go out in the way of salvage tugs or high speed launches, a harbour at which there would be listening posts watching for signals.

Canada Shipping Act
On the British Columbia coast the places which can be so described include only Vancouver, Victoria, Nanaimo, Port Alberni and Prince Rupert, the public harbours. The steamship lines get around this regulation because of the words "place to place". On a trip north to Prince Rupert, a ship carrying 400 passengers going 500 miles-a thousand mile round trip-can easily avoid carrying a radio operator by stopping at some point; before reaching the 90 limit mile they can stop at a little logging camp or some little fishing village, or any place where there is a float, just as long as they stop and start again thus beginning a new voyage. I submit that the intent of the act is being evaded by that practice, and the people of British Columbia want to see that provision complied with. When we are in committee I intend therefore to move an amendment to section 406, changing the word "place" to the words "public harbour", in order that these provisions, which are sensible provisions, as applying to the type of ship that can go on voyages of various lengths, shall apply to voyages between public harbours, places from which aid could go to a ship in distress.
The ship operators, of course, being aware that they are evading the spirit of the law, tell the public that all is well because they now have these new radiotelephones and the masters and men can operate them without radio operators and can call help immediately in case of need. This may sound plausible enough, especially to an ordinary civilian who realizes what a great advance the radiotelephone is over the old radiotelegraph using the Morse code. The actual fact of the matter is that the very opposite is the truth as far as the use and practicability of the radiotelephone and radiotelegraph are concerned on the British Columbia coastal ships.
In the first place the radiotelephone is a much more intricate mechanism than the ordinary radiotelegraph sending machine. It is much more likely to get out of order, because it is more intricate, and neither the skipper nor the mate has the skill to repair such an apparatus. Then tihe radiotelephone, both the sen-ding and receiving machines, must be accurately tuned. Mistuning, as you know from experience with radio sets in your own homes, blurs speech and signals. In the third place, unintelligible speech over a radiotelephone may well ruin the whole point of the message. We all have had this happen when listening to the radio. Occasionally we may have heard ourselves on the radio, and at times I am sure we have been amazed at the way we blurred and slurred our own
speech, even we who are accustomed to speaking. How much more likely is a mate or a master, in time of emergency, rushing to a radiotelephone with which he has had very little practical experience, to blur and slur his speech and make his message unintelligible to anyone receiving it at the other end.
Ordinary radio interference from other electrical apparatus on the ship affects a radiotelephone signal very much more thah a radiotelegraph signal, because of the very much -higher frequency of radiotelephony. The same is true of static. We all know the effect of static on most radio sets, especially car radios; and that, too, is a factor to be considered in the dispatch of messages by radiotelephone. Our British Columbia coast is described by those with radio experience as being extremely spotty, by which they mean that reception is good at times but that in -the same spot an hour or two later it may be very bad. This also leads to the condition known as fading, under which a radiotelephone message simply fades out, another experience I think most of us have had with our own radios at home.
The next feature is the nervousness and excitement of the operator, if he is not a competent radiotelephone operator. If the boat has run on a rock or has run down a fishing boat, and the master or math 'goes to operate the fairly complex radiotelephone, it is quite likely he will turn the .wrong switch or do the wrong thing or forget part of the routine necessary in the operation of such a machine.
Another -possibility is the jamming of a distress call by the many fishing boats and tug boats on- our coast, all of which use the same channel as the coastal steamers. The radiotelephone is -a great thing for the tug boats and fishing boats on our coast, enabling them to maintain contact with their base and to pass messages back and forth. The one ohannel we have is filled almost all the time; and any coastal ship attempting to break into that channel with a distress signal would have very little hope of getting through.
Another point is the failure of the radiotelephone channel allotted to coastal ships in British Columbia to reach the deep-sea ships which are also plying our coast and which operate on another frequency. But the last and most important reason that the radiotelephone operated by the master or mate is absolutely inadequate and insufficient for real protection is this. The most important thing about sending a message from a ship is not so much that it be sent but that it be received. The very
Canada Shipping Act

best distress message sent out would be valueless unless somewhere in the area someone else was listening. Of course the classic instance of that was the Titanic disaster. At the time the California was only twenty-five miles away, but the operator had gone to bed and did not hear the distress call. If every coastal ship on the British Columbia coast with radio service is to have a radiotelephone on the wall, operated by the master or mate when there is need to send out a call, there will be very few people to receive such messages. Other ships will be similarly equipped, and there will be no real listening watch.
On the other hand, a radiotelegraph operated by an operator-or even better still, both radiotelephone and radiotelegraph-provides complete protection both in regard to dispatching messages and in being fairly certain that those messages will be received. In the first place the radiotelegraph as such is a simple mechanism, not likely to be out of order and easily repaired. In the next place it sends a clear and distinct signal. Probably everyone here who has used the radio at all knows that many times when you cannot get a particular program you can hear, loud and clear, the dash-dot-dot of some distant radiotelegraph station. There is also much less interference and static because of the lower frequency used in sending these messages. No jamming by fishing boats is possible, because the operators on fishing boats and tugs are not telegraphers; they use the radiotelephone. The operators on deep-sea ships are all telegraphers and all listen. Finally radiotelegraph is much more reliable, because it is operated by a man whose job it is to run that mechanism and do nothing else. In case the mechanism breaks down, he can repair it. The actual sending of messages is a. job for which he is trained; and above all, since this is his only job, he is also maintaining a listening watch for signals from other ships in the area, something which is not done with the radiotelephone, and so can take action when a distress signal is received.
When our coastal ships in British Columbia are forced to carry an operator they often try to save a little money-though the cost of one operator carried on a ship is not very great- by making him perform other duties. They say, "Oh, that man is just sitting up there all day long. That is a lazy man's job. We must make him freight clerk or purser," using him as an operator only when the ship is wrecked and he has to send a signal. Of course the objection there is the main objection to the radiotelephone, the fact that when he has other employment he can not maintain the listening watch which all ships should maintain

to help others in distress. Then, naturally, more and more of his time will be devoted to his other job and he will not spend the necessary time on the maintenance of his equipment, while at the same time he will get rusty in his technique. The argument that it is a lazy man's job could be applied equally to the lookout at the masthead, but what ship could do without him? It could be applied also to the firemen in the fire hall or the policeman on patrol. There are jobs where it seems the chief function is to wait for an emergency which everyone hopes will not occur; but when it does the man must be trained and ready to deal with it.
One other point was raised by the companies in objecting to the campaign waged by the daily press at home for proper enforcement of the Canada Shipping Act as far as radio operators are concerned. They said it was possible for the operator to be a purser or freight clerk if he would rig up a loudspeaker attached to the radiotelephone in his operator's cabin, and as he worked away at his figures as a purser or clerk he could be listening with one ear to the broadcast coming from behind. I have been on these coastal boats a great deal and I have seen these loud-speakers rigged up. If the man is working he has it turned down, because he cannot add figures and at the same time listen to a noisy radio. But far more frequently you will find, rather than the loudspeaker attached to the radiotelephone set being on, it is attached to an ordinary radio bringing music from Vancouver or Victoria, completely ruining the value of such a hookup.
Actually the present law, if properly enforced, does not permit this dual job of radio operator and freight clerk or purser. The Canada Shipping Act itself provides that in those cases where a radio operator must be carried by a ship he must maintain a daily log, and must make an entry in that log every fifteen minutes when on duty. That is an excellent thing. To begin with, it shows that he is awake, and it also permits him to time any messages he receives with respect to weather or traffic in the area, or any distress signals. The actual time schedule of an operator on duty is given in appendix 4 of the Canada Shipping Act, showing that if this law is enforced and the operator is required to keep a log with entries every fifteen minutes, obviously he cannot have another job such as purser or freight clerk.
Therefore, while complimenting the minister on the excellent amendments he has brought forward to other parts of the Canada Ship-

Canada Shipping Act
ping Act, I feel that one thing has been overlooked. I refer to a minor change in section 406 of the act, where provision is made for radio operators on coastal ships. When the appropriate time comes in committee of the whole I intend to move a simple amendment; that this word "place" be changed to "public harbour", which I think was the intent of those who framed the legislation in the first place.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words on second reading. A principle is being introduced for the first time into the Canada Shipping Act which affords ground for some dissatisfaction.
Since the war, Canadian legislation has lost the characteristic of applying to everyone at all times and in all circumstances-a characteristic which has made Canadian legislation, and that of countries upon which our form of government is patterned, admired throughout the world. Gradually there have crept into the legislation of this parliament, while we have been struggling to get back to parliamentary government as distinct from government by the executive, devices whereby legislation, although enacted by parliament, may be modified by the executive. The executive has retained the power to modify legislation in such a manner that the executive finds itself master of all situations. A bill introduced a little while ago affecting foreign exchange control was susceptible to amendment by the minister to whom the control was entrusted to such an extent that the legislation was practically obliterated. In that instance it was competent to the minister at any time to repeal rules, regulations and orders which determined how currency should be admitted and administered, thereby permitting the minister in spite of the rules and regulations to determine what should be done.
I find in this bill the same spirit expressing itself. It is a dangerous departure from what has always been a characteristic of Canadian legislation; thus the law becomes uncertain and subject to the whim of the administrator to such an extent that at no time can anyone be sure just what the law is; nor is he capable of observing it, because it may be amended at any time without notice.
To give point to what I have just said, I would refer the house to section 11 of the bill.

And so on. My point is that this amendment to the shipping act enables the minister at any time he sees fit to wipe out, as it were, those sections of the Canada Shipping Act which have been relied upon for many years for the protection of the lives of seamen and of people travelling by sea.

speechtext: Before the hon. member goes further, may I make the comment that this section is much the same as section 78 of the United Kingdom act. speechtext: That is just the ground of my complaint-that the socialization of the British act, which places in the hands of the administration the power to alter legislation whenever the executive deems it wise to do so, impairs the fundamental continuity and certainty of legislation.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: But the British section has been in existence for quite some time; it is not a recent amendment.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934

If the minister examines the British amendment carefully I believe he will find that it follows a trend which has become quite marked in British legislation in the last few years. It is a trend which is detrimental to our legislative system, because it undermines the stability of legislation by making one law apply to one group of people and then, if the administration does not wish to apply it to the next group, operates in such a maimer that all the administration has to do is to pass an order in council, with the result that the law is suspended or changed. I submit that this is an introduction, into this realm at least, of a new principle, one which cannot
Canada Shipping Act

but make for uncertainty and insecurity at a time when security and certainty in legislation are characteristics that are highly desirable.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we proceed with the clause by clause discussion of this bill I should like to make a few remarks. It is not my intention to make elaborate comments upon the proposed amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, as eventually we will have the privilege of discussing the bill further in detail once we reach the clause by clause discussion stage.
My intention in rising at this time is to draw the attention of the committee to what I consider to be a few shortcomings in the bill which deeply concern me. First, however, I should like to make a few remarks on the definitions contained in this bill. The other place, as we call it in this house, has seen fit to amend the definition of home-trade voyage. I am in full accord with what was decided upon by the senate, but I am not prepared to accept the amendment passed in the senate with regard to inland voyage and minor waters of Canada. I doubt the desirability of changing these two definitions. I submit that the definition of inland voyage should be read most carefully in connection with the regulations covering certificates of inspection. We are giving to masters of ships the privilege of sailing in zones in which they could not sail before. I submit that this committee should give careful consideration to the fact that by amending the definitions of inland voyage and of minor waters of Canada we are extending the certificates of competency given to masters of ships without compelling them to increase their knowledge of navigation and of the waters in which they will be permitted to sail in the future.
The bill before us provides for a new definition of sailing ship intended to comply with the recommendations of a commission headed by Mr. Justice Cannon which sat in 1942 to consider navigation of small boats on the St. Lawrence and to recommend proposed amendments to the act in order to bring these ships within the act. May I be permitted at this stage to read two of the three recommendations made by Mr. Justice Cannon on October 20, 1944. I quote:
Certificates:	Since there are still a number
of masters on vessels of under 150 tons gross, especially on the smaller vessels, which have no certificates and cannot pass the necessary exam-

inations, because of lack of education; it is suggested that if the regulations concerning "service certificates" could be amended so that this type of certificate could be still available by undergoing an oral examination, up to January, 1948. The masters not at present holding any certificate could all avail themselves of this opportunity; since the majority of them have quite a number of years of experience.
The third conclusion in the report of Mr. Justice Cannon deals with a special class for vessels engaged in the St. Lawrence coastal trade. This reads:
Special class of vessel:	It is suggested that
motor driven vessels of under 150 tons, gross, classed as sailing vessels under the steamship inspector's regulations, may be put into a special class of "motor vessels" having their own particular regulations concerning equipment, _et cetera, since they are actually of a special class, but not properly defined and therefore as far as equipment and certificates are concerned, never positive whether they are "motor vessels" or "sailing vessels."
At this point I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that up to today we have adopted in this special trade on the St. Lawrence a system of tolerance. We gave a classification of sailing ship to ships which were not sailing ships at all, but were really and truly motor ships. We gave this special privilege to ships under 150 tons, and that is my explanation of why the Hon. Mr. Justice Cannon in his report confined his conclusions and recommendations to this type of vessel under 150 tons gross tonnage. However, Mr. Chairman, I feel that by accepting the wording of Mr. Justice Cannon's report as it is, the government and the department are not doing the right thing. We are creating a special class of ships, taking into consideration not the territorial waters in which they are to sail, not the dangers and other difficulties of navigation which they may encounter in this trade, but rather the size of the ships. To my mind it is the same thing as if the registrar of motor vehicles in Ontario told a man that he did not need a driving licence if he drove a jeep, but that he must have one if he drove a truck or a bus. I believe sincerely that if the master of a ship is not qualified to sail a ship of 151 tons he is not qualified to sail a ship of 148 tons. Therefore I respectfully suggest that we create a new class for this special type of vessel, but that we do not limit this class to a certain tonnage, but rather take into consideration the territorial waters in which the ship will be permitted to sail, and require of the masters of these ships and the owners the qualifications and the necessary requirements as to provision for life-saving equipment and the prevention of fires that must be required of a ship engaged in that trade.

Canada Shipping Act
On certain types of vessels it is impossible to insist on the various requirements laid down by the Canadian steamship inspection board. For example, we are creating a new class of ship as far as certificates of competency are concerned, but we put these ships, even one under 150 tons, as far as inspection is concerned, in the same class as a ship of 1,000 tons. The inspection regulations say that a ship with a crew of seven persons on board must have two lifeboats, each of which is large enough to accommodate the whole crew of the ship. One of these lifeboats should be class one while the other should be class three. But you cannot demand this requirement of the owner of a ship of 50 tons because there is not room on the boat deck of that ship to locate the two lifeboats.
In forming this new class I respectfully suggest, as I said before, that we should take into consideration the waters in which the ship is to sail, the dangers to navigation, the trade in which she is to be engaged, and the number of crew she is to carry. If we want to help this trade on the St. Lawrence, help the coastal trade of Canada, we shall have to face the problem in this way, otherwise we will not improve it.
I again suggest that this class should not be limited to 150 tons. I think that the amendment passed by the senate relating to inland voyages should help to convince the government and this committee that it should be so. As a matter of fact the other place has just granted to masters of ships engaged theretofore in the trade on the lakes and inland waters of Canada permission to sail their ships from Father Point to the west point of Anticosti island. We have only to increase this limit of the inland waters a few miles more and we cover the whole of the St. Lawrence coastal trade. If we are to use territorial limits, this limit should include the whole of the gulf of St. Lawrence including Chaleur bay. If we are going to ask the masters of these ships to hold certificates of competency we should be very careful in outlining the requirements necessary for the attainment of such certificates. I myself do not think that we should require from the future masters of these ships that they know celestial navigation. As a matter of fact, today we are asking these captains who are to sail only in the St. Lawrence that they know how to navigate by celestial bodies. Well, I should like somebody to point out to me a spot on the St. Lawrence river where you can have a good horizon, good enough to navigate by celestial bodies. We teach them to use a sextant, which they are not even compelled to carry on their ships. What is the use of having them learn the course which
shows them how to handle a sextant when they are not compelled to have them on their ships when they go to sea?
In making regulations having to do with these new certificates we should ask these men to learn how to adjust their compass and to know pilotage. We should insist on pilotage; we should insist that they know pilotage regulations in the St. Lawrence river and the international rules of the road. We should teach them navigation in sight of the coast. That is the only type of navigation they will be called upon to use. We are wasting our time if we ask them to know geometry, to know how to use a sextant, which means of navigation they will never use in their trade.
I also wish to offer a few comments on the amendment brought in by the senate to the clause covering desertion. I am not in accord with the hon. member for Skeena who yesterday criticized this amendment by the senate. I ask hon. members of this committee to consider carefully the expressions in this amendment where we require that, before the crew can go on a legal strike, the ship be placed in a port of safety or rather in security. I think we should be very careful, when we give power to the harbour master or the master of a ship to determine whether or not the ship is in security, not to give them the privilege of extending that to tidal harbours or tidal ports.
Personally I know of one example where a ship suffered heavy damage and caused very severe damage to a sister ship when her lines broke owing to the carelessness of the crew. She was damaged when the tide ran out because the lines broke. When I ask this committee to consider carefully this amendment we are dealing with, I am not at all trying to take something away from seamen, whom I want to see afforded the best treatment, but I am insisting that we should be very careful not to give them in this act something which will finally work against themselves. I am thinking at the moment of danger to the lives of seamen, whom we want to protect today.
The same can be said of ports where there is no shelter. No one knows when a storm may come up and a ship will break her lines and be cast adrift, and ninety-nine times out of a hundred she will ram a sister ship tied at the same wharf. Therefore, if we are going to leave the clause as it stands, I would impress upon the minister the necessity of bringing to the attention of the officers of his department the importance of this matter and giving instructions to the harbour master not to consider ships in security, unless he is satisfied that in case of emergency tlfere will be at
Canada Shipping Act

least a skeleton crew on hand to look after the ship, should a storm or any other unforeseen event take place.
I come now to the definition of Canadian ship in the shipping act. I have heard many hon. members, both in the house and outside, ask in very convincing words for the establishment in this country of a Canadian merchant marine. I agree with them, and their case has my full support and sympathy. But how can we have a Canadian merchant marine without having a Canadian ship? I have only to quote section 3 of the act of 1934 as it stands today to convince this committee that if we want to be logical with ourselves when we ask for a Canadian merchant marine we should have a Canadian ship. Section 3 of the act of 1934 reads:
Every vessel, which is about to be built or is being built or equipped in Canada and which, when completed, launched and/or equipped will be a ship registrable in Canada as a British ship, .may, as to a vessel about to be built, and shall, as to a vessel being built or equipped, be recorded, pending registration, under an assigned number and a temporary name in the office of the registrar of British ships at the port in Canada at or nearest to which such vessel is about to be built or is being built or equipped.
Further, in the interpretation of the terms at the beginning of the act, item 5, section 2, "Interpretation", the words British ship are defined as follows:
"British ship registered in Canada," and "ship registered in Canada" means a ship registered in Canada either under the provisions of this act or under the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Acts before the coming into force of this act.
Further still, a ship registered in accordance with this act is also defined, the definition being at item 8, "Interpretation", section 2, of the Canada Shipping Act:
"Registrar" means a registrar of British ships.
This act does not give us a legally true Canadian ship. Moreover, may I be permitted to read part of the Canadian Citizenship Act, section 47, in which we set out the necessary qualifications that one must have to become a Canadian citizen. Section 4, part I of the citizenship act reads:
A person, born before the commencement of this act, is a natural born Canadian citizen:-
(a) if he was born in Canada or on a Canadian ship.
Again in section 5 of the same act we find the following:
A person, born after the commencement of this act. is a natural-born Canadian citizen:-
(a) if he is born in Canada or on a Canadian ship.	[DOT]

In the same act we find in the interpretation section 2, item (b), where Canadian ship is defined:
A "Canadian ship" means a "ship registered in Canada" within the meaning of the Canada Shipping Act, 1934.
I have just proved, I think, that no such Canadian ship exists under our Canada Shipping Act, 1934. What I have just said comes, in my opinion, into conflict with the Canada Shipping Act as it stands today. I am also of the opinion that the effect of amending the act in order to give us a Canadian ship does not come into conflict with the merchant shipping agreements passed by the imperial conference of 1930 where common status was given all ships of the British commonwealth. The aim of the imperial conference of 1930, in relation to merchant shipping, is set out clearly in the following quotation from the report of the conference on the Operation of dominion legislation on merchant shipping, 1939. I quote the following excerpt, found at pages 12 and 13, giving the terms of reference of the conference. At page 12:
Merchant Shipping
12.	The imperial conference of 1926 also considered the general question of merchant shipping legislation. On this subject the conference pointed out that, while uniformity of administrative practice was desirable and, indeed, essential as regards the merchant shipping legislation of the various parts of the empire, it was difficult to reconcile the application, in their present form, of certain provisions of the principal statute relating to merchant shipping . . .
At page 13, section 13:
13.	On further examination of the problems involved, it appeared more convenient that the committee and the special subconference should be organized as a single conference. After consultation between the respective governments this view received general acceptance, and the terms of reference to the present conference accordingly include, in addition to those set out above, a reference -
"To consider and report on the principles which should govern, in the general interest, the practice, and legislation relating to merchant shipping in the various parts of the empire, having regard to the change in constitutional status and general relations which has occurred since existing laws were enacted."
Just one other citation from the report of the same conference of 1929, at page 40, item 97, where common status is defined as follows:
97. Common Status

(a) There should be agreed uniform minimum qualifications for ownership to govern the admission of ships to registry in all parts of the British commonwealth of nations. The provisions of section 1 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894, would appear to form a suitable basis for that purpose.

Canada Shipping Act
I want to emphasize the words "suitable basis".
(b)	Ships complying with these agreed qualifications for ownership and registered in any part of the British commonwealth of nations will possess a common status for all purposes and will be entitled to the same recognition as is now accorded to British ships.
Further, it is my contention that my suggestion is therefore not in contradiction to or in disagreement with the draft agreement as to British commonwealth of nations merchant shipping, and I beg to quote this draft agreement as reported in the report of the imperial conference of 1930, part I, summary of proceedings. At page 31, I find the following :
Part I
Common Status Common Qualifications
Article 2-(1) No ship shall be registered in any port within the British commonwealth so as to acquire the status and recognition mentioned in paragraph (2) of this article unless it is owned wholly by persons of the following description, namely:-
(a)	Persons recognized by law throughout the British commonwealth of nations as having the status of natural-born British subjects;
(b)	Persons naturalized by or in pursuance of the law of some part of the British commonwealth;
(c)	Persons made denizens by letters of denization; and
(d)	Bodies corporate established under and subject to the law of some part of the British commonwealth and having their principal place of business nothin the British commonwealth.
(2) Every ship so owned and duly registered within the British commonwealth shall possess a common status for all purposes and shall be entitled to the recognition usually accorded to British ships.
Then article 3 proceeds to state on what special items it was desired that this common status be given as far as registry was concerned. I quote just the first and last part of the sentence in article 3:
Article 3-The laws, regulations, forms and procedure relating to the matters following, that is to say:-
There is then given the enumeration of the various items mentioned, and the section *continues:
. . . shall be substantially the same throughout the British commonwealth and so far as possible be based on part I of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894.
I particularly draw the attention of the committee to the adverb "substantially."
I could go on quoting further excerpts from this report of the imperial conference, but I think I have given enough of them to satisfy this committee that there is no conflict whatsoever between my suggestion and what was agreed upon in this draft agreement of 1930.
I also beg to draw to the attention of this committee the fact that the British commonwealth merchant shipping agreement was signed in London on December 10, 1931; that is, just one day before the Statute of Westminster which, by sections 2, 3 and 5, granted to Canada the right to legislate without taking any notice of the Colonial Laws Validity Act.
In closing my remarks on this subject, I wish to quote Doctor Maurice Ollivier's "Problems of Canadian Sovereignty", at page 138, in which he says:
So, the dominion exercised that right

He is talking of the right given by the Statute of Westminster.
-by passing a new merchant shipping act in 1934.
By passing that act, the dominion has exercised its absolute right of legislating with respect to ships, wherever they may come from, when they happen to be in Canadian waters; it has exercised its right to legislate as to ships registered in Canada-
I want to emphasize the words "right to legislate as to ships registered in Canada."

whether they be in Canadian waters or elsewhere, subject in that case to local laws when the ships happen to be in non-Canadian waters or ports.
There is therefore no doubt whatsoever that this parliament has the right to legislate or has the legislative power necessary to create this much needed Canadian ship. I hope also, in closing my remarks, that once this Canadian ship is given to Canada, our government will take steps to protect this Canadian ship while engaged in the Canadian trade. Part IV of the draft agreement of 1930 gave equal treatment to all ships of the British commonwealth in the following terms, by article 10, to be found at page 32 of the report of the 1930 conference:
Each part of the British commonwealth agrees to grant access to its ports to all ships registered in the British commonwealth on equal terms and undertakes that no laws or regulations relating to seagoing ships at any time in force in that part shall apply more favourably to ships registered in that part, or to the ships of any foreign country, than they apply to any ship registered in any other part of the commonwealth.
Article 11 provides:
While each part of the British commonwealth may regulate its own coasting trade, it is agreed that any laws or regulations from time to time in force for that purpose shall treat all ships registered in the British commonwealth in exactly the same manner as ships registered in that part, and not less favourably in any respect than ships of any foreign country.
Canada Shipping Act

Article 12 of the same draft agreement reads:
Nothing in the present agreement shall be deemed-
(i) to derogate from the right of every part of the commonwealth to impose customs tariff duties on ships built outside that part . . .
I beg the committee to note that this draft agreement gave us the privilege of imposing customs tariff duties on ships built outside this country. By introducing legislation tending to reserve the coastal trade of Canada to our Canadian ships, either by means of customs tariff duties on foreign-built ships or otherwise, then and only then will Canada encourage the creation and maintenance of a Canadian merchant marine and develop a stable and flourishing shipbuilding industry in this country.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I sincerely hope that the government will immediately consider the desirability of introducing further amendments to our shipping act in order to give us, together with, a Canadian merchant marine, a true Canadian ship which will soon fly a true Canadian flag on the seas of the world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
I should like to say just a few words on this act as it applies to fishing craft, and some of the definitions concerning them.
By this act it will be noted that ships of more than ten tons register are classified as steamships if they have any means of propulsion other than sail. That is a restrictive feature on our fishing fleet, which has its tradition in sail, though of recent years it has in some measure modernized itself, first by putting a donkey engine on the deck to hoist the sails and anchor, and more recently, with the growing demand for fresh fish and the need for speed in getting to and from the fishing banks, by a trend toward propulsion. As a matter of fact, almost all the schooners and ships in the fishing fleet are now equipped with diesel engines; but they are the same type of ship as we had twenty years ago-the hull form is the same; they have the masts and sails, though they are not used to the same extent, and they are substantially and basically the same type of ship as when they had no means of propulsion other than their sails.
It seems an unusual hardship on the fishing fleet to classify these boats as steamships and therefore require them to submit to all the regulations applying to steamships, including the qualifying requirements for officers and particularly engineers. There are also the inspections during the building of a ship which must be conformed to, and in that way an additional hardship is imposed. Ships are

built today in exactly the same way; the same kind of timber, the same skill and the same designs are used as were used twenty or thirty years ago, when Nova Scotia developed traditionally as the province that specialized in wooden ships and iron men.
This provision seems to bear most heavily on the engineers, who are in fact fishermen who in many instances were forced to leave the work in the dories and fishing boats and take work on board what we call a fishing schooner or what might be termed a mother ship. They have done so by reason of disability, or for some other cause. They have become proficient in looking after diesel engines and other propulsion units, to the point where they are just as competent as an engineer holding higher qualifications, but under this act and the regulations they are debarred if they are not qualified.
I must say the minister has seen fit in certain cases to exercise some leniency and discretion in allowing such people to qualify. I have brought two or three cases to his attention, and he has made it possible for the men to undergo a special examination by the board of steamship inspection and obtain temporary certificates permitting them to operate. This is possible, however, only in special circumstances, and it is a dispensation in all such cases. Under the act there is no coverage which would permit these men to qualify, and in time I believe that will result in an unnecessary hardship upon the fishing fleet which is struggling along, doing its best to conform to the regulations and to progress. Nevertheless, with its roots deep in history and tradition which go back to the sailing days it is pretty difficult for our fishermen to change quickly; so I would ask the minister to give us time in that respect and extend all the leniency and discretion within his power.
I would say this is a good bill; there is no question about that. It will work for the over-all betterment of our mariners and the merchant marine. In time I am sure our deep-sea fishing will develop to the point where we can conform to all the regulations in this measure, but at the moment we cannot; it is just impossible. So we shall have to be shown some leniency during the transition period, which may last for a considerable time.
To say, as the bill does, that all ships of less than ten tons are sailing ships and all those of more than ten tons are steamships, if they have any method of propulsion other than sail, is drawing the line too fine and placing it too low, in my interpretation of this act. A ten-ton boat does not engage in

Canada Shipping Act
fishing on the deep sea, and therefore plays very little part in the deep-sea fishing industry. In the schedule to the act respecting the international labour conference, however, I note that the dividing line is drawn at vessels of 200 tons gross register. It seems to me that would be much more fitting, and would give us a certain latitude which is needed.
I should like to bring another point to your attention, Mr. Chairman, in connection with sick mariners' benefits. These come under part V of the act; but I should like to refer to the matter at this time, if I may. There are two points in particular which affect us, and from the speech of the hon. member for Skeena I would gather that the same things apply on the west coast. One feature is that fishermen who leave a Canadian port and for some reason-disability, failure of some kind, or something else-are obliged to seek shelter in a foreign port, do not become eligible for sick mariners' benefits in that foreign port. On the west coast that would apply to fishermen leaving Vancouver ports and touching in Alaska or the United States. On the east coast our boats occasionally touch the United States; they frequently go to Newfoundland and St. Pierre and Miquelon, and there is the possibility that they may go to other foreign ports.
With particular reference to our east coast fishermen, it is traditional and part of the industry that they take on bait in Newfoundland. In the spring of the year it is often hazardous to get to Newfoundland. There are often ice floes and other difficulties of weather and navigation. Recently, with the trend whereby, to some extent, our fishing fleet is manned by Newfoundlanders, it has been the practice to have some of our Nova Scotia vessels lie over in Newfoundland through the winter months, and set out on their first fishing trip of the year from a Newfoundland port, before they touch a Canadian port. They leave from Newfoundland, catch their cargo of fish-if they are lucky- and return that cargo to a Canadian port.
Under the interpretation of the applicable sections of the act, these fishermen have not been able to qualify for merchant seamen's benefits, presumably because the act reads that the first payment for the calendar year must be made before the ship makes its first fishing voyage in that year. This seems to be interpreted to mean that the ship must leave a Canadian port on its first trip in order to qualify for merchant seamen's benefits.
This appears to draw an argument almost to a point of absurdity. One of our schooners registered in Lunenburg, but lying over for the winter in Newfoundland, will leave Newfoundland, go to the banks, take its catch of fish, return to Lunenburg and find that it is disqualified for merchant seamen's benefits. But if that same schooner leaves Newfoundland, touches at the extreme eastern end of Nova Scotia, then proceeds to the fishing banks and returns its catch to Nova Scotia, it can qualify for merchant seamen's benefits. By so doing, it increases its cost of operation, and seems to put itself at a disadvantage which is in no way justified. I would strongly urge the minister to give this case exceptional consideration. I understand that it is administered by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He is familiar with the circumstances; but I thought this would be a good time to discuss the matter. If an amendment to the act is necessary I should be pleased to bring it in, and I am confident hon. members would support it.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would speak briefly along the lines followed by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg when he referred to the amendment whereby boats of ten tons are classed as steamships, and come under the same regulations. There are several amendments which I feel will greatly inconvenience fishermen of Charlotte county and other sections of the maritime provinces. This amendment is one which I am sure will be discussed by fishermen in that section of the country, and which will be strongly opposed.
In the section of the maritimes from which I come will be found hundreds of small islands, ledges and shoals where the sardine fisheries operate, and where the movement of tide is very rapid. The water is shallow to a point where many sections of that area are still uncharted. Many of the channels navigated by fishing boats today cannot be found on the charts supplied by the department in Ottawa. Experience, and years of cruising in these dangerous waters by men who began in their youth to take part in that business, have qualified them to carry on in that section. I feel, however, that boats used exclusively in passenger and freight coastal service in any part of the maritime provinces, or any other section of the dominion, should come under government inspection. Indeed, perhaps in many cases that inspection should be more rigid than it has been in the past.
I remember speaking briefly about two years ago on this same matter, wThen I referred to the loss of the Robert Cann in 1946 off Grand Manan island. The Robert Cann was an old boat. Anyone who has had experience on salt water would know it was not fit for
Canada Shipping Act

the service it was trying to render at that time. However, there was a scarcity of that type of boat, and it was allowed to carry on. Consequently in February, 1946, a tragedy involving thirteen persons took place.
I say the boat was not fit for the job, because these thirteen persons who were lost when the boat sank got into a lifeboat sixteen feet long, and crossed the bay of Fundy on the same night. They perished while crossing. I feel the regulations covering boats of this type should be quite rigid. The ordinary fishing boat, however, should in my opinion be exempt from these regulations. I say that because today in all branches of the fishing industry of the maritime provinces the boats being used are much larger than they were ten years ago. The great percentage of boats would come under the regulation we are now discussing.
Then, I should like to touch briefly upon the matter of loss of life and loss of boats in the maritimes. I believe if we go through the records we shall find that the hard, tough types of men are in this business in the maritimes; most of them came up the hard way, and the loss of life and of boats and equipment in the maritime provinces is as small as in any other part of the world. In fact down there today one would find only a very small percentage of boats insured. I would say that 99 per cent of the boats in the fishing industry today in the maritime province do not carry insurance. It is seldom that we hear of the loss of a boat.
Then, I would discuss briefly the matter of inland waters. I can remember as a boy hearing this discussion take place on many occasions. That section in which the sardine industry is carried on has always been known as inland waters; there is a different classification altogether when one goes outside the bay of Fundy.
Some time in the thirties-I do not remember the exact year-a regulation came into force making it necessary that masters of boats of ten tons or over have certificates.
I remember the circumstance well, because I was on the water at that time. One of the qualifications was that the applicant must have been the skipper of a boat of ten tons or over for a period of ten years before making application for a licence. I happened to be one of the few who had had his name on the register of a boat for that number of years. I made application and received my certificate; but at that time there were many men from the same section in which I live who were better qualified than I but

who failed to obtain their certificates at that time, owing to the fact that they had not had their names on the registers of boats of ten tons or over for a period of ten years. Those little technical points have made it difficult in that part of the country for fishermen and boatmen to carry on.
I would refer now to the regulation of the department whereby life-rafts, dories, lifeboats, fire-extinguishers and all equipment of that kind must be aboard a fisherman's boat today before it can pass inspection. I have seen boats in my section of the country' so laden with this equipment that, by the time they had aboard all that was necessary, there was very little room left for nets, winches, drags and all the other equipment, required for fishing purposes.
