maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: On many of those boats in my section of the country there would be only two men employed, and three on a good-sized boat.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: If the hon. member looks at the section, he will see that this makes provision for regulations. The regulations have not yet been made, and I am sure that a condition such as he refers to will be taken into consideration in making the recommendations.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: Will these boat drills take place before an inspector of this department, or is it a boat drill that will be carried on on board under the supervision of the master of the ship and recorded in the log only?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: It would be under the master of the ship, I am informed. But the regulations would cover a situation such as that.

Section agreed to.
Sections 37 to 39 inclusive agreed to.

On section 40-Minister may relieve ships from compliance with this part.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: This is another clause like clause 11 to which I directed some remarks on the second reading of the bill. Roughly, this section is similar to section 11 of the bill; it refers to section 133a of the act; it gives to the minister certain powers. This section gives to the minister, on the recommendation of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection, the power to delete substantial portions from the statute.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: But only in case of emergency.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Well, how clear is that? The minister will note that the section we are considering, which is section 40 of the bill, but which is to be section 488A of the shipping act, is in these terms:
Notwithstanding anything in this part, the minister, on the recommendation of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection, may relieve any ship registered in Canada or the owner of any such ship from compliance rvith any of the provisions of this part or regulations made thereunder relating to steamship inspection, excepting provisions relating to radiotelegraph installations in ships, in any specific case of emergency where the minister may deem it necessary or advisable in the public interest, to such extent, in such manner and upon such terms as he may consider proper in the circumstances . . .
The minister will not think me facetious if I tell him that the wonderful capacity of the government to create emergencies does not leave me wholly satisfied that an emergency may not be created without a great deal of justification. In this instance we are dealing with part VII of the Canada Shipping Act, which is under the heading "Safety," and it is in this part that all measures providing for the safety of the crew, the passengers and the ship are enacted. Under section 40 of this bill the minister, upon the recommendation of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection -who as a rule is not unfriendly to the minister-may delete nearly all these safety provisions from the statute. Glancing over these provisions hurriedly, I see that they include safety and inspection certificates; provision as to safety convention, ships not registered in Canada; limited and other voyages; overloading passenger ships; safety precautions, radio equipment and so on. It is the story of the protective devices which the experience of long years of seafaring have placed upon the statute books.
I admit mournfully that within the last three or four years the government has enacted legislation like this. That is, the government has placed it within the power of the executive

Canada Shipping Act
to thwart by executive determination, which is by order in council, legislation embodied in statutes. As a result, there is no fixity in the legislation; there is no permanency in it. Legislation ceases to be applicable to all persons in all cases. It may be applied to A and it may not be applied to B if the governor in council has the approval of the chairman of the board of steamship inspection. No one knows what it takes to convince the chairman of the board of steamship inspection, and no one knows exactly what the law is, because at all times and without notice it is subject to change.
My criticism is levelled at this particular statute. Section 40 is evidence of a tendency which, if persisted in, is bound to undermine the respect Canadians have had for statute law, because it will be variable, indeterminate, and subject to alteration without notice to the parties. I am going to ask the minister if he will be good enough to explain to the committee why such drastic changes are being introduced into this act. I hope he will find a better reason than saying the parliament in Britain has recently passed similar legislation.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
I think I can give my
hon. friend more than one good reason why it is being placed in the statute in this manner.
In the first place, this section, as well as the one of which my hon. friend complained this afternoon, was discussed at quite considerable length in this house under the transitional powers act.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I am aware of that.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. gentleman raised the same point

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I did.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
but certainly members of his party raised the point. Those two sections were fully discussed at that time, and it was stated by myself that they would be inserted in the Canada Shipping Act in the amendments to be brought down this session.
This order in council has been in force since 1942. and has worked well. Had it not been in effect, it would have been impossible to keep ships moving. My hon. friend says it is not sufficient to say there is a similar provision in the United Kingdom act. I am not giving that as a reason, but we all like to turn to the British parliament and to cite what is being done there, where they have had far more experience than we have had in maritime matters.
Then, if my hon. friend had read a little further-though I am sure he has read it all- he would have seen that the danger of which
he complains is mitigated substantially by these words:
. . . but the minister shall not relieve any ship or owner from compliance with any such provision to such extent or in such manner as would permit any ship to proceed to sea or make any voyage or trip in an unseaworthy condition, that is to say, unfit by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of undermanning, overloading or improper loading, to proceed to sea or make any such trip or voyage without serious danger to life.
During the debate on the transitional powers measure, I think I was asked how many such exemptions had been given. I do not recall at the moment how many there were, but the number was not great over the years the provision has been in force. Certainly I am able to say that no accident or death or injury to anyone arose by reason of the order in council.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: But would the minister say why it is necessary in peacetime to perpetuate a measure to which we all bowed under the exigencies of war? During the war we yielded up the ordinary processes of democratic government. But now that the war is over, why should the minister be entitled to declare whether or not there is an emergency. He may be a very good and able man; but why should an individual be able to tear up a statute, simply because he believes there is an emergency. We all know that, amid the stresses of the type of life to which the minister and others have devoted their many talents, emergencies of one kind of another come forward rapidly. What is the reason today for deleting from a statute many of these lifepreserving measures, many of these measures which have become law as a result of the experience to which the minister has referred, measures that have been on the statute books unchallenged and untouched until the war?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Because if this section were not included or if it were not approved, many ships and their cargoes would be tied up and unable to move. I can think of one particular instance where I was called late at night by the master of a ship, who pointed to the fact that he had a huge cargo which would be subject to loss unless he were given an exemption under this section. On the matter being referred to the chairman of the steamship inspection board he reported it was a case of emergency, and recommended that section 488 should not be applied and that the exemption should be given.
If that provision had not existed by virtue of the War Measures Act the ship would have been tied up until a complete inspection could have been made. There are times when it is
Canada Shipping Act

not possible for inspectors to make the annual inspections to see that the boilers, hulls and equipment are in first-class condition. Again, when it appears to the satisfaction of the chairman of the steamship inspection board, who communicates with the inspector in the locality where the ship is situated, that it is a case of emergency, he so recommends to the minister who, as a rule, accepts the advice; because, speaking for myself, I have not the technical knowledge which would permit me to make a decision. I must rely upon the advice I receive from the steamship inspector.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I do not wish to overstate the case, nor do I wish to be disrespectful to the minister or to say things which would be disagreeable to him. But I must tell him in all sincerity that I think an application of the principle he is advocating is subversive of the whole theory of statutory enactment, and of the rule of law. That rule of law cannot in any respect be dependent upon the whim or good temper or honesty of an individual. A statute containing a provision like this ceases to be a rule of law, and becomes a rule of an individual. That is one of the dangers confronting us today.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member for Stanstead that in the operation of ships some flexibility has to be allowed for the exercise of discretion by the minister, or the chairman of the steamship inspection service. I have in mind a vessel out on whaling operations, which is due to come in for inspection on September 1. Their normal season does not end until probably the middle of October.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: That is not what we are discussing.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
There
should be some discretion left.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: That is not what we are discussing. We are giving to the minister the right to tear page after page out of the Canada Shipping Act. It is a pure act of volition, depending upon his judgment and integrity-

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: In a case of emergency.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not often I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Stanstead; but I do at this time.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: With some regrets.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Although, as I say, I do not often find myself in agreement with him, I have great respect for the sincerity of his

point of view and also for his judgment. The minister said that the order in council under the War Measures Act was in effect since 1942. It came into effect in wartime, when we were short of ships, when there was an emergency and when the ordinary rules of safety did not and could not apply. Why today, three years after the war is over-or in the future, perhaps ten years after the war is over-a provision like this should remain, I do not know.
The minister referred to one case where he was called up during the night where a ship with cargo was laid up and unable to move. The question is: Why was that allowed to happen? Why was not the ship examined before she was loaded? If one is going to say, "Well, we have to get out, even if the ship is not inspected; we will have the minister give us a permit in order to sail"-surely that is making a monkey out of the law. Even with my slight knowledge of law, I suggest that would be poor law indeed.
In a committee today I made an attempt to have a slight variation made in a section in another bill. My suggestion was to use an expression somewhat similar to the one I see at the top of this bill-"notwithstanding anything in the preceding section". I was told that was not good law. Here we find the wording goes this far: "notwithstanding anything in this part". It is not a section, but a whole part of the act. The minister could throw the whole act under the table, and give permission to do things the act does not permit. I suggest that is not good law, although it has been in effect since 1942. There was good reason for it at that time, but that reason does not apply today.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: Yes, the reason is the same today as it was then.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: Only last year a company in my constituency had a freighter built in Nova Scotia. Certain equipment required could not be installed in the particular area where it was built. Because of this section in the act, the owners were allowed to bring the boat across the bay of Fundy to the New Brunswick side in order to have the equipment installed. In cases of that kind this section is most helpful.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
Surely there must have been something in the Canada Shipping Act prior to these provisions which have been mentioned. Inspectors must have had some degree of leeway; because I know I have been told to lay off chipping a double bottom, because I was going right through. All that

Canada Shipping Act
was keeping me from the water was rust. I could see that, of course. There must have been some leeway at one time or another prior to these provisions being brought in. I wonder if this is necessary.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I should like to add a little to what has been said by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. You must have a certain amount of flexibility. For example, you might have a highly perishable cargo which would be ruined if not moved immediately, which is often the case. It might be that a ship was awaiting inspection but was needed right away in order to move that cargo. It will be noted that section 488A does not take away responsibility for the safety of the ship, the loadline or anything else. The law must be complied with, otherwise the owner and the master are responsible. I believe that a certain amount of flexibility should be permitted and the master given some discretion in the matter. Shipping, particularly sea shipping, is different from any other industry. I think this is an important section.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
I want to make a point in connection with this section in support of the amendment that I said on second reading I was going to move in connection with radiotelegraph service. It will be noted that this section grants great powers to the minister with relation to relieving a ship from various inspections which it should pass, but the minister is not given any leeway with regard to one service. In about the fifth line of the section it says:
. . . excepting provisions relating to radiotelegraph installations in ships . . .
I draw those words to the attention of the committee, because they show clearly that those who drew up the Canada Shipping Act put that service and that inspection above all others. The minister cannot relieve a ship of any responsibility in that connection.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I tried to get a copy of the merchant shipping act of Great Britain from the library but was unable to do so. Apparently there is only the one copy and it is out.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I thought the minister had it.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: He is innocent.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
The minister has told us that this proposed amendment follows along the lines of the merchant shipping act of Great Britain. Has the same wording been adopted here as was adopted in Great Britain? I
presume that this was by way of amendment to the merchant shipping act and I should like to know when the amendment was made.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: The amendment to the merchant shipping act of the United Kingdom was made in 1906. I can speak only from memory, but the wording is not exactly the same; there is some variation.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: As I read this section, it does not state who shall determine whether a specific emergency exists.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: The minister does that.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: It says the minister may deem it necessary or advisable in the public interest, but it does not say he is the person who determines that a specific emergency exists. Is that the intention?

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: The intention is that, on representations made by various masters or ship owners or steamship inspectors, he may relieve the ship from compliance with this part.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
It seems to me that subsection 1 is drafted to apply only to a period of emergency, and in my opinion a period of emergency should be capable of definition. Subsection 2 reads:
Subsection one shall have force and effect only during such period or periods as the governor in council may determine.
That means that any time can be considered a period of emergency. We should have more information as to what creates or causes an emergency when we are asked to give these wide powers to the minister. That explanation has not been given. There were some fantastic statements made in regard to what this section might prevent being done. The hon. member for Charlotte mentioned a ship which had not had its machinery installed and which could not. be moved from one place to another in order to have the machinery installed. Surely that is a fantastic thing, because that ship was not going to sea.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I beg your pardon, the ship was going to sea.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: It could not go to sea without its machinery.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
It could go across the bay of Fundy.
Canada Shipping Act

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: I think I know that bay nearly as well as my hon. friend. This is important legislation and surely it cannot be justified by the feeble arguments that have been put forward.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: It appears to me that the hon. member for Vancouver East is of a suspicious nature. Apparently he assumes that an individual who happens to own a boat is a capitalist and it is better to put him out of business. You cannot order things at sea the way you can order a taxi business in Vancouver. Emergencies arise and the minister must be given some power.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext: If the hon. member for Comox-Alberni did not feel so guilty he would not think I was suspicious. I realize that emergencies do occur at sea, and it is because I do not want emergencies to occur that I do not want the minister to be given these wide powers that may send ships to sea that are not worthy to go to sea.

maintopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT AMENDMENTS TO ACT OF 1934
speechtext:
It is a dangerous principle to substitute the minister for the board of steamship inspection. We had a measure like that temporarily during the war. The law should provide for the safety of the public.
Progress reported.

In the table on the next two pages (No. 10) an attempt is made to bring together in one statement and under uniform headings the transactions of all governments in Canada on a calendar year basis. (See explanatory note below table).
Using the statistical methods appropriate to the calculation of the National Income and Expenditure (which differ somewhat from the accounting methods used by governments) it is estimated that during the calendar year 1947 federal, provincial and municipal governments took in as revenue $4,058 million and spent $3,141 million, leaving an overall surplus of $917 million of which $774 million was attributable to the federal government and $143 million to the provincial and municipal governments. The year before the federal government showed a deficit of $228 million and provincial and municipal governments a surplus of $101 million.
Expenditures by governments may be divided into two main categories : expenditures for the purchase of goods and services, and so-called transfer payments, i.e., family allowances, old age pensions, the greater part of the interest on the public debt, veterans' benefits, etc., which do not arise from current production of goods and services. The first category represents the demands which governments place on the annual output of the nation. Transfer payments, on the other hand, simply add to the sums available for spending or saving by the recipients.
During the calendar year 1944, at the peak of Canada's war effort, the federal government absorbed 38% of that year's production of goods and services and provincial and municipal governments an additional 5%. By 1946 federal expenditures on goods and services had fallen to 9% of the gross national product, while similar provincial and municipal expenditures had risen to 6%. During the calendar year 1947 provincial and municipal expenditures continued to rise and federal government expenditures to fall, so that now, as in pre-war years, provincial and municipal governments together absorb a larger share of current output than the federal government.

8.	The personal income tax which yielded $659,828,000 retained its position as the largest single source of revenue. The substantial tax reductions which became effective on January 1 and July 1, 1947, resulted in a revenue lower by $34,702,000 than that of the previous year. This was a reduction of only 5%, a very small decline in relation to the extensive reduction in rates. The continuing high revenue from this source reflects the increased incomes and the high level of employment throughout the year.
9.	Corporation income tax and excess profits tax, both levied on business profits, yielded a total of $591,161,000, a decline of $96,329,000 from the previous year's total. The corporation income tax yield of $364,131,000 was $125,339,000 more than in the previous year and indicates the result of the increase from 18% to 30% in the corporation income tax which became effective on January 1, 1946, as well as the high level of business profits in 1947. The excess profits tax yield of $227,030,000 was $221,668,000 less than in the previous year, showing the effects of the change made in the tax on January 1, 1946, as well as the reduction in the rates of tax.

Revenues under the headings "Taxes on Dividends and Interest" and "TAXES ON RENTS AND ROYALTIES" are derived from special taxes, largely on income going to non-residents of Canada, levied under authority of section 9b of the Income War Tax Act. In 1947-48 revenue under this heading amounted to $35,889,000, an increase of $5,753,000 over the previous year. This increase reflects higher dividend payments during the year and the extension of the 5% tax to dividends from wholly-owned subsidiaries going abroad to parent companies, which became effective on April 30, 1947.
11.	Succession duties, yielding $30,828,000, showed a marked increase of $7,252,000 over the previous year. Although there has been an increase in revenue from this source every year since succession duties were first levied in 1941, the sharp increase in 1947-48 was largely due to the fact that seven provinces have rented this field of taxation to the Dominion and consequently there were no provincial duties in these provinces to be deducted from the higher Dominion rates which have prevailed since January 1, 1947.
12.	Net revenues from customs import duties reached the all-time high of $293,012,000, exceeding the receipts of the previous year by $55,657,000. This very high revenue reflects the heavy import trade resulting from the extensive capital investment program, the high level of consumer purchasing power, and the widespread demand for goods, factors which were so much in evidence during the year under review and which contributed so largely to the serious depletion of the country's supply of United States dollars.
13.	Excise duties, which are levied exclusively on alcoholic beverages and tobacco products, brought in a total revenue of $196,794,000, an increase of $750,000 over the previous year. The revenue from alcoholic beverages declined slightly and that from tobacco products increased moderately, by $953,000. As in previous years, the smokers' contribution to the federal treasury was considerable, with the overall revenue from tobacco products (including the yield of the additional taxes imposed under the Excise Act on tobacco, cigarettes, cigarette papers and tubes), amounting to $177,141,000. This is 7-2% of the total revenue from taxes.
14.	Under the heading "Excise Taxes" are included a wide variety of taxes levied on commodities and services under the Excise Tax Act. The most important of these taxes from the point of view of revenue is the sales tax which yielded a gross revenue of $383,012,000 during 1947-48, an increase of $54,939,000 over the previous year. This increase of 16-7% reflects the increased supply of 

The Budget-Appendix
commodities available for consumption during the year and the generally higher price level. Since November 17, 1947, this tax has not applied to electricity and gas used in dwellings.
15.	The second largest revenue source among the excise taxes is the tax on tobacco products which yielded $68,606,000. Although this amount is $7,712,000 less than that for the previous year, this decline in revenue is almost entirely due to a variation in the procedure for remitting the tax which resulted in revenue being included in March 1947 which would normally have been reported in April, thus increasing the revenue for 1946-47 at the expense of 1947-48.
16.	The revenue from several excise taxes showed marked increases during the year. With increased production due to more abundant supplies of sugar, the revenue from soft drinks increased 27 * 5% and that from candy and chewing gum increased by 37 -7%. The revenue from the tax on automobiles and tires and tubes almost doubled in 1947-48 due to the greater production of automobiles during the year and to the increase in the tax which became effective on November 18, 1947. The tax program announced on that date also resulted in increased revenue from phonographs, radios and tubes, and from electrical and gas appliances. Among those items which yielded reduced amounts were cigarette papers and tubes, toilet preparations and soap, and transportation and communications. The tax on sugar which was repealed on November 17, 1947, yielded a smaller revenue than the previous year and a clean-up amount of $2,208,000 is shown for the gasoline tax which was repealed as from April 1, 1947. Refunds of excise taxes declined from $29,845,000 in the previous year to $10,685,000, which represents at more normal level of refunds than that which prevailed during the war and immediate post-war years.

26.	For the first time in ten years, interest charges on the public debt fell below the previous year, a direct result of the reduction in debt during the year. 27.	The largest single increase during the year-$47,128,000-was in the total of payments to Provinces, including statutory subsidies and payments under the tax agreements. The increase in the tax agreement payments, amounting to $28,117,000, is a result of the payment during 1947-48 of $63,000,000 due under the wartime tax agreements. The remainder is largely attributable to the payment of $8,031,250 to each of the Provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan arising out of the Natural Resources settlement.

28.	Family allowances payments rose by $18,024,000, or about 7%, mainly as a result of the changes in the income tax provisions relating to dependetn children, which became effective as from the beginning of 1947 although there is, of course, a steady rise from month to month due to natural increase. The increase in old age pensions and pensions for blind persons of $13,642,000, which represents more than a 30% increase from the previous year, indicates the effect of the higher rate of pensions and revised income qualifications. Government contributions to unemployment insurance and administrative expenses under the Act showed a moderate increase. During the year the costs of National Selective Service were combined with administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
29.	A major drop in expenditures relating to veterans accounted for almost one-half of the total reduction in ordinary and demobilization and reconversion expenditures during the fiscal year. Payments of war service gratuities and re-establishment credits, alone, declined from $318,325,000 in 1946-47 to $84,135,000 in 1947-48. There was also a drop of nearly 50% in the costs of treatment. Pension costs relating to veterans of World Wars I and II, on the other hand, continued to increase.

The further withdrawal from wartime controls is reflected in the substantial reductions in expenditures under the headings of agricultural subsidies, price control and subsidies directly related to price control. 71.	Indirect or contingent liabilities of the Government include the guarantee of the deposits maintained by the chartered banks in the Bank of Canada, guarantees of certain bond issues and bank loans, commitments under housing legislation, and certain other guarantees.
Guaranteed Bond Issues
72.	Bonds and debenture stocks guaranteed by the Government were outstanding in the hands of the public in the amount of $521,949,171 as at March 31, 1948, a decrease of $45,005,355 during the year. This decrease was caused chiefly by the redemption of two Canadian National Railways 3% bond issues: the $20,000,000 issue due February 1, 1952 was called for redemption on February 1, 1948 and the $25,000,000 issue due February 15, 1953, was called for redemption on February 15, 1948.
Guaranteed Bank Loans-
(1)	Farm Improvement Loans
73.	Under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944, the Government guarantees loans made by the chartered banks to farmers for certain authorized purposes. The amount of the guarantee is limited to 10 per cent of the aggregate principal amount of the guaranteed loans made by each bank. Figures for March 31, 1948, are not yet available, but at February 28 a total of 41,722 such loans had been made to a total amount of $33,631,453.71, and the Government's contingent liability at that date was $3,363,145.37, compared with $1,564,865 at March 31, 1947.
(2)	Veterans' Business and Professional Loans
74.	Under the provisions of the Veterans' Business and Professional Loans Act, the Government guarantees loans made for certain purposes by the chartered banks to veterans domiciled in Canada. The total of such loans is limited to $25,000,000, and the Government's guarantee is limited to 25 per cent of the loans made by a bank if that bank's total loans do not exceed $1,000,000 and to 15% of the loans mamde by a Bank in excess of $1,000,000. At December 31, 1947, the Government's contingent liability for loans made under this Act amounted to $1,216,571.12.
(3)	Guaranteed Bank Loans to Acadia Coal Company
75.	P. C. 1188 of March 29, 1946, authorized the Government to guarantee the extension of bank loans not exceeding $730,000 to the Acadia Coal Company Limited to assist the company in opening and developing the McBean seam on a fully mechanized basis. At March 31, 1948 loans for the maximum amount authorized were outstanding.
(4)	Guarantees under Part II, Export Credits Insurance Act
76.	Under authority of P. C. 4690 dated November 12, 1946, the Minister of Finance was authorized on behalf of the Government of Canada to guarantee under the provisions of the Export Credits Insurance Act the guarantee of the Republic of China of the payment by Ming Sung Industrial Company, Ltd., of the cost of Canadian-produced goods and Canadian services to a maximum

The Budget-Appendix
amount of $12,750,000 to be advanced by Imperial Bank of Canada, The Bank of Toronto and The Dominion Bank, subject to an agreement dated October 30, 1946, between the Company and the said Banks, and to guarantee the securities given by the Ming Sung Industrial Company Ltd., for repayment of amounts drawn against credits established by the Banks in accordance with the agreement.
This guarantee was made at the request of the Government of China, which itself has guaranteed the payments to be made by the Company and the securities to be given by the Company and has undertaken to indemnify the Government of Canada against loss in connection with the guarantees so requested.
As of March 31, 1948, letters of credit issued and special credits established by the said banks in favour of the Ming Sung Industrial Company totalled $9,997,320.00. Total payments by the banks under these letters of credit or special credits amounted to $6,106,850.87, and the liability of the Government at the end of the fiscal year is, therefore, $6,106,850.87.
Guarantees on Land Assembly Projects undertaken by Lending Instititions
77.	A new provision was added to The National Housing Act, 1944, at the 1947 Session of Parliament to empower and encourage lending institutions to acquire suitable blocks of raw land within or adjacent to urban centres and develop this land into serviced lots for housing construction. Subject to the lending institutions undertaking to develop the land acquired and sell this land under terms and conditions satisfactory to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Corporation is authorized to guarantee the total investment of the lending institutions in the land and development, including interest on the investment at a rate not to exceed two per cent compounded annually. In return for the guarantee the lending institutions agree to pay to the Corporation any amount recovered from the sale of such land, in excess of the total investment and the amount of the accrued interest. At the termination of the Agreement any unsold land in a project is to be conveyed to the Corporation.
At the end of March, 1948 agreements had been entered into with various lending institutions respecting six land assembly projects. The total estimated investment in these projects was $1,197,267.03. No claims have been made to the Corporation under the provision of the guarantee.
